title: Between Two Worlds: Language, Identity, and Belonging

dialogue.speaker: Aliya
dialogue.text: I've been thinking about language a lot lately — about what it means to speak three languages but feel fully at home in none of them.

dialogue.speaker: Marcos
dialogue.text: I know that feeling. I grew up speaking Portuguese at home, Catalan at school, and Spanish in the street. I sometimes joke that I think in all three simultaneously and don't entirely belong to any one of them.

dialogue.speaker: Aliya
dialogue.text: That's exactly it. In terms of fluency, I speak Kazakh, Russian, and English. But emotionally — the language I dream in, the language I reach for when I'm scared or happy — that's Kazakh. And yet English is the one that's opened the most doors professionally.

dialogue.speaker: Marcos
dialogue.text: There's something strange about that, isn't there — having your professional identity shaped by a language that isn't emotionally yours? I feel that too with English. It's the language of my career, but it sometimes feels like a costume rather than a skin.

dialogue.speaker: Aliya
dialogue.text: That's a very evocative way to put it. Though I've also noticed that different languages don't just describe things differently — they make me a slightly different person. I'm more direct in English. More indirect and formal in Kazakh.

dialogue.speaker: Marcos
dialogue.text: That's fascinating — and it resonates with the research on this. There's evidence that bilinguals and multilinguals can show measurably different personality profiles depending on which language they're using. The language you're using primes you for certain cultural frameworks.

dialogue.speaker: Aliya
dialogue.text: In relation to English specifically — do you ever feel pressure to sound "native"? To erase your accent?

dialogue.speaker: Marcos
dialogue.text: I used to. When I was working in London, I was very self-conscious about my accent. But I've come to think: my accent is part of who I am. It tells people where I'm from, and that's not something to apologise for.

dialogue.speaker: Aliya
dialogue.text: I completely agree. And from the perspective of World Englishes, there is no single correct English. The British or American norm isn't intrinsically superior — it's just historically dominant.

dialogue.speaker: Marcos
dialogue.text: Exactly. I find it frustrating when people treat non-native speakers as linguistically inferior. As if the additional cognitive work of navigating multiple languages were a disadvantage rather than an enormous skill.

dialogue.speaker: Aliya
dialogue.text: There's good evidence that multilingualism has cognitive benefits — better executive function, enhanced metalinguistic awareness. In the context of global communication, being multilingual is a massive advantage.

dialogue.speaker: Marcos
dialogue.text: And yet there's still so much linguistic prejudice. People are judged by their accent in job interviews, by their written style in applications, by how native-like their English sounds. With regard to equality, these are real barriers.

dialogue.speaker: Aliya
dialogue.text: Yes. And for many people, the pressure to adopt the dominant language fully means suppressing or losing the ones that carry their emotional life. That's a real cost that often goes unacknowledged.

dialogue.speaker: Marcos
dialogue.text: I think that's why language policy matters so much — in education, in workplaces, in public life. The question of which languages are valued and which are marginalised isn't just linguistic. It's political.
